newsitem.title: USA: Conn. managed health care seen hurting quality.
newsitem.headline: Conn. managed health care seen hurting quality.

text.p: Managed care has cut medical costs and paperwork for Connecticut consumers, but many patients and physicians think it is also hurting health care quality and access, according to a survey released Thursday.

Connecticut physicians overwhelmingly believe that managed care has shifted administrative and cost burdens onto them, and that the system is lowering costs mainly by not paying bills, the study by the Center for Research and Public Policy shows.
The research was commissioned by the Connecticut State Medical Society.

"This research shows that there are benefits to managed care, but they are primarily in the areas of lowering premiums and reducing paperwork for patients," said Dr. Michael Deren, president of the Connecticut State Medical Society.

"The areas that are of greatest concern to both physicians and patients are quality and access," Deren said in a statement. "And as the only advocates for patients in the system, we want to make it clear that those areas can quite literally mean the difference between life and death."

While 55 percent of the consumers surveyed believe managed care is containing medical costs, some 57.3 percent agreed with the statement "We're moving from quality medical care to adequate medical care."
Some 66 percent agreed that "Managed care is causing confusion and frustration among consumers and patients."
Advantages cited were lower price, no claim forms, and low co-pays.
Among the perceived disadvantages were limited doctor selection, and limited or flawed services.
Nearly half of all respondents favored state government legislation creating oversight of managed care.
Among the physicians surveyed, almost three-quarters disagreed with the statement, "Managed care has created better patient care."
Managed care is defined as a system that aims to control costs partly by controlling a patient's access to medical services, often by the use of a gatekeeper.

The potential regulation of managed care is currently being debated in the Connecticut legislature. Physicians and consumer groups favor state regulation, while insurance companies oppose it. --Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224
